[[File:YieldSurfacerhoxitheta.svg|right|300px|thumb|Surfaces on which the invariants <math>\xi</math>, <math>\rho</math>, <math>\theta</math> are constant. Plotted in principal stress space. The red plane represents a meridional plane and the yellow plane an octahedral plane.]]

'''Lode coordinates''' <math>(z,r,\theta)</math> or '''Haigh–Westergaard coordinates''' <math>(\xi,\rho,\theta)</math>.<ref name="aci">Menetrey, Philippe; Willam, K. J.; 1995, "Triaxial Failure Criterion for Concrete and its Generalization", ''Structural Journal'', American Concrete Institute, Volume 92, Issue 3, pages 311-318, DOI: 10.14359/1132</ref> are a set of [[Invariants of tensors|tensor invariants]] that span the space of [[Real number|real]], [[Symmetric tensor|symmetric]], second-order, 3-dimensional [[tensor]]s and are [[Isomorphism|isomorphic]] with respect to [[Stress space|principal stress space]]. This [[Right-hand rule|right-handed]] [[Orthogonality|orthogonal]] coordinate system is named in honor of the German scientist Dr. Walter Lode because of his seminal paper written in 1926 describing the effect of the middle principal stress on metal plasticity.<ref>Lode, Walter (1926), „Versuche über den Einfluß der mittleren Hauptspannung auf das Fließen der Metalle Eisen, Kupfer und Nickel“ ["Experiments on the influence of the mean principal stress on the flow of the metals iron, copper and nickel"], ''Zeitschrift für Physik'', vol. 36 (November), pp. 913–939, DOI: 10.1007/BF01400222</ref> Other examples of sets of tensor invariants are the set of principal stresses <math>(\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3)</math> or the set of kinematic invariants <math>(I_1, J_2, J_3)</math>. The Lode coordinate system can be described as a [[cylindrical coordinate system]] within principal stress space with a coincident origin and the z-axis parallel to the vector <math>(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3)=(1,1,1)</math>.

==Mechanics invariants==
The Lode coordinates are most easily computed using the mechanics [[Invariants of tensors|invariants]]. These invariants are a mixture of the invariants of the [[Cauchy stress tensor]], <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}</math>, and the [[Cauchy stress tensor#Stress deviator tensor|stress deviator]], <math>\boldsymbol{s}</math>, and are given by<ref name="asaro2006">Asaro, Robert J.; Lubarda, Vlado A.; 2006, ''Mechanics of Solids and Materials'', Cambridge University Press</ref>

:<math> I_1 = \mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})</math>

:<math> J_2 = \frac{1}{2}\left[\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2) - \frac{1}{3}\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})^2\right] = \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}\left(\boldsymbol{s}\cdot\boldsymbol{s}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\lVert \boldsymbol{s} \rVert^2</math>

:<math> J_3 = \mathrm{det}(\boldsymbol{s}) = \frac{1}{3}\mathrm{tr}\left(\boldsymbol{s}\cdot\boldsymbol{s}\cdot\boldsymbol{s}\right)</math>

which can be written equivalently in [[Einstein notation]]

:<math> I_1 = \sigma_{kk} </math>

:<math> J_2 = \frac{1}{2}\left[\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2) - \frac{1}{3}\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})^2\right] = \frac{1}{2}s_{ij}s_{ji} = \frac{1}{2}s_{ij}s_{ij} </math>

:<math> J_3 = \frac{1}{6}\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{pqr}\sigma_{ip}\sigma_{jq}\sigma_{kr} = \frac{1}{3}s_{ij}s_{jk}s_{ki} </math>

where <math>\epsilon</math> is the [[Levi-Civita symbol]] (or permutation symbol) and the last two forms for <math>J_2</math> are equivalent because <math>\boldsymbol{s}</math> is symmetric (<math>s_{ij}=s_{ji}</math>).

The gradients of these invariants<ref name="kayenta">Brannon, Rebecca M.; 2009, ''KAYENTA: Theory and User's Guide'', Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, New Mexico.</ref> can be calculated by

:<math> \frac{\partial I_1}{\partial \boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \boldsymbol{I} </math>

:<math> \frac{\partial J_2}{\partial \boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \boldsymbol{s} = \boldsymbol{\sigma} - \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right)}{3}\boldsymbol{I}</math>

:<math> \frac{\partial J_3}{\partial \boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \boldsymbol{T} = \boldsymbol{s}\cdot\boldsymbol{s} - \frac{2J_2}{3}\boldsymbol{I}</math>

where <math>\boldsymbol{I}</math> is the second-order identity tensor and <math>\boldsymbol{T}</math> is called the Hill tensor.

==Axial coordinate <math>(z)</math>==

The <math>z</math>-coordinate is found by calculating the magnitude of the [[orthogonal projection]] of the stress state onto the [[Hydrostatic pressure#Hydrostatic pressure|hydrostatic]] axis.

:<math>z =  \boldsymbol{E_z} \colon \boldsymbol{\sigma} = \frac{\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{I_1}{\sqrt{3}} </math>

where

:<math> \boldsymbol{E_z} = \frac{\boldsymbol{I}}{\lVert \boldsymbol{I}\rVert} = \frac{\boldsymbol{I}}{\sqrt{3}}</math>

is the unit normal in the direction of the hydrostatic axis.

==Radial coordinate <math>(r)</math>==

The <math>r</math>-coordinate is found by calculating the magnitude of the stress deviator (the [[orthogonal projection]] of the stress state into the deviatoric plane).

:<math>r = \boldsymbol{E_r}\colon \boldsymbol{\sigma} = \lVert \boldsymbol{s} \rVert = \sqrt{2 J_2} </math>

where

:<math>\boldsymbol{E_r} = \frac{\boldsymbol{s}}{\lVert \boldsymbol{s} \rVert}</math>

:{| class="toccolours collapsible collapsed" width="50%" style="text-align:left"
!Derivation
|-
|The relation that <math>r=\sqrt{2J_2}</math> can be found by expanding the relation

:<math> r = \frac{\boldsymbol{s}}{\lVert \boldsymbol{s} \rVert}\colon\boldsymbol{\sigma}</math>

and writing <math>\sigma</math> in terms of the isotropic and deviatoric parts while expanding the magnitude of <math>\boldsymbol{s}</math>

:<math> r = \frac{\boldsymbol{s}}{\sqrt{\boldsymbol{s}\colon\boldsymbol{s}}} \colon \left( \boldsymbol{s} + z \boldsymbol{E_z} \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\boldsymbol{s}\colon\boldsymbol{s}}} \left( \boldsymbol{s}\colon\boldsymbol{s} + z \boldsymbol{s}\colon\boldsymbol{E_z}\right)</math>.

Because <math>\boldsymbol{E_z}</math> is isotropic and <math>\boldsymbol{s}</math> is deviatoric, their product is zero. Which leaves us with

:<math> r = \frac{\boldsymbol{s}\colon\boldsymbol{s}}{\sqrt{\boldsymbol{s}\colon\boldsymbol{s}}} = \sqrt{\boldsymbol{s}\colon\boldsymbol{s}} </math>

Applying the identity <math>\boldsymbol{A}\colon\boldsymbol{B} = \mathrm{tr}\left(\boldsymbol{A}^T\cdot\boldsymbol{B}\right)</math> and using the definition of <math>J_2=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}\left(\boldsymbol{s}\cdot\boldsymbol{s}\right)</math>

:<math> r = \sqrt{\mathrm{tr}\left(\boldsymbol{s}\cdot\boldsymbol{s}\right)} = \sqrt{2 J_2}</math>
|}

is a unit tensor in the direction of the radial component.

==Lode angle – angular coordinate <math>(\theta)</math>==
[[File:Lode Angle Approximation Comparison.svg|right|400px|thumb|This plot demonstrates that an intuitive approximation for the Lode angle is the relative position of the middle principal stress <math>\lambda_m</math> with respect to the low and high principal stresses.]]

The Lode angle can be considered, rather loosely, a measure of loading type. The Lode angle varies with respect to the middle [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalue]] of the stress. There are many definitions of Lode angle that each utilize different [[trigonometric functions]]: the positive sine<ref name=chak>Chakrabarty, Jagabanduhu; 2006, ''Theory of Plasticity: Third edition'', Elsevier, Amsterdam.</ref> (It is '''incorrect (false)''' information that Chakrabarty defines shear stress mode angle with sin(Teta). Chakrabarty adopted Lode parameter with opposite sign than it has in the original Lode paper from 1926, see Page 59, formula (3) in the book «Chakrabarty, Jagabanduhu; 2006, Theory of Plasticity: Third edition, Elsevier, Amsterdam.». Effectively Chakrabarty shear stress mode angle is defined with -sin(Teta) just like it did for the first time Novozhilov in his work from 1951, Novozhilov 183-194, «О СВЯЗИ МЕЖДУ НАПРЯЖЕНИЯМИ И ДЕФОРМАЦИЯМИ В НЕЛИНЕЙНО УПРУГОЙ СРЕДЕ» (On relations between stresses and strains in non-linear elastic media) from 1951. The first work in which arguments and discussion is delivered why it is wise and useful to define shear stress mode angle with sin(Teta) is the Ziolkowski’s work «Parametrization of Cauchy Stress Tensor Treated as Autonomous Object Using Isotropy Angle and Skewness Angle» from 2022, <nowiki>https://et.ippt.pan.pl/index.php/et/article/view/2210</nowiki>. Accepting definition with sin(3Teta) in fact means that ''pure shears'' are accepted as ''comparison reference states'', what has serious consequences.), negative sine,<ref name="neto2008">de Souza Neto, Eduardo A.; Peric, Djordje; Owen, David R. J.; 2008, ''Computational Methods for Plasticity: Theory and Applications'', Wiley</ref> and positive cosine<ref name="han1985">Han, D. J.; Chen, Wai-Fah; 1985, "A Nonuniform Hardening Plasticity Model for Concrete Materials", ''Mechanics of Materials'', Volume 4, Issues 3–4, December 1985, Pages 283-302, doi: 10.1016/0167-6636(85)90025-0</ref> (here denoted <math>\theta_s</math>, <math>\bar{\theta}_s</math>, and <math>\theta_c</math>, respectively)

:<math> \sin(3\theta_s) = -\sin(3\bar{\theta}_{s}) = \cos(3\theta_c) = \frac{J_3}{2}\left(\frac{3}{J_2}\right)^{3/2}</math>

and are related by

:<math> \theta_s = \frac{\pi}{6} - \theta_c 
        \qquad \qquad
        \theta_s = -\bar{\theta}_s
</math>

:{| class="toccolours collapsible collapsed" width="50%" style="text-align:left"
!Derivation
|-
|The relation between <math>\theta_c</math> and <math>\theta_s</math> can be shown by applying a trigonometric identity relating sine and cosine by a shift

:<math> \cos(3\theta_c)=\sin(3\theta_s)</math>
:<math> \cos(3\theta_c)=\sin\left(\left(3\theta_s - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) + \frac{\pi}{2} \right)</math>
:<math> \cos(3\theta_c) = \cos\left(3\theta_s - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) </math>.

Because cosine is an [[Even and odd functions|even function]] and the range of the [[Arccosine|inverse cosine]] is usually <math>0\leq\cos^{-1}(\theta)\leq 1</math> we take the negative possible value for the <math>\theta_s</math> term, thus ensuring that <math>\theta_c</math> is positive.

:<math> 3\theta_c = \pm \left( 3\theta_s - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) </math>
:<math> \theta_c = \frac{\pi}{6} - \theta_s </math>
|}

These definitions are all defined for a range of <math>\pi/3</math>.

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center"
|- 
!
!Stress State <math>\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \sigma_3</math>
!<math>\theta_s</math>
!<math>\bar{\theta}_s</math>
!<math>\theta_c</math>
|-
| range || || <math> -\frac{\pi}{6} \leq \theta_s \leq \frac{\pi}{6} </math> || <math> -\frac{\pi}{6} \leq \theta_s \leq \frac{\pi}{6} </math> || <math>0 \leq \theta_c \leq \frac{\pi}{3} </math>
|-
| Triaxial Compression (TXC) || <math> \sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 = \sigma_3 </math>||<math> -\frac{\pi}{6} </math> || <math> \frac{\pi}{6} </math> || <math> \frac{\pi}{3} </math>
|-
| Shear (SHR) || <math>\sigma_2=(\sigma_1+\sigma_3)/2</math>|| <math> 0 </math> || <math> 0 </math> || <math> \frac{\pi}{6} </math>
|-
| Triaxial Extension (TXE) || <math>\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 \geq \sigma_3</math>|| <math> \frac{\pi}{6} </math> || <math> -\frac{\pi}{6} </math> || <math> 0 </math>
|-
|}

The unit normal in the angular direction which completes the [[orthonormal basis]] can be calculated for <math>\theta_s</math><ref name="brannon2007">Brannon, Rebecca M.; 2007, ''Elements of Phenomenological Plasticity: Geometrical Insight, Computational Algorithms, and Topics in Shock Physics'', Shock Wave Science and Technology Reference Library: Solids I, Springer-New York</ref> and <math>\theta_c</math><ref name=bigoni2004>Bigoni, Davide; Piccolroaz, Andrea; 2004, "Yield criteria for quasibrittle and frictional materials", ''International Journal of Solids and Structures'', Volume 41, Issues 11–12, June 2004, Pages 2855-2878, doi: 10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2003.12.024</ref> using

:<math> \boldsymbol{E_{\theta s}} = \frac{\boldsymbol{T}/\lVert\boldsymbol{T}\rVert - \sin(3\theta_s)\boldsymbol{E_r}}{\cos(3
\theta_s)}
  \qquad
  \boldsymbol{E_{\theta c}} = \frac{\boldsymbol{T}/\lVert\boldsymbol{T}\rVert - \cos(3\theta_c)\boldsymbol{E_r}}{\sin(3\theta_c)}
</math>.

==Meridional profile==

[[File:plasticity models meridional profile.svg|right|400px|thumb|This plot shows a typical meridional profile of several plasticity models: [[von Mises yield criterion|von Mises]], [[Drucker-Prager yield criterion|linear Drucker–Prager]], [[Mohr-Coulomb theory|Mohr–Coulomb]], [[Gurson yield criterion|Gurson]], and [[Yield surface#Bigoni.E2.80.93Piccolroaz yield surface|Bigoni–Piccolroaz]]. The upper portion of the plot depicts yield surface behavior in triaxial extension and the lower portion depicts yield surface behavior in triaxial compression.]]

The [[Zonal and meridional|meridional]] profile is a 2D plot of <math>(z,r)</math> holding <math>\theta</math> constant and is sometimes plotted using scalar multiples of <math>(z,r)</math>. It is commonly used to demonstrate the pressure dependence of a [[yield surface]] or the pressure-shear trajectory of a stress path. Because <math>r</math> is [[Non-negative#non-negative and non-positive|non-negative]] the plot usually omits the negative portion of the <math>r</math>-axis, but can be included to illustrate effects at opposing Lode angles (usually triaxial extension and triaxial compression).

One of the benefits of plotting the meridional profile with <math>(z,r)</math> is that it is a geometrically accurate depiction of the yield surface.<ref name="brannon2007" /> If a non-isomorphic pair is used for the meridional profile then the normal to the yield surface will not appear normal in the meridional profile. Any pair of coordinates that differ from <math>(z,r)</math> by constant multiples of equal [[absolute value]] are also isomorphic with respect to principal stress space. As an example, pressure <math>p=-I1/3</math> and the [[Von Mises stress]] <math>\sigma_v = \sqrt{3J_2}</math> are not an isomorphic coordinate pair and, therefore, distort the yield surface because

:<math> p = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}z </math>

:<math> \sigma_v = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} r </math>

and, finally, <math> |-1/\sqrt{3}| \neq |\sqrt{3/2}|</math>.

==Octahedral profile==

[[File:plasticity models octahedral profile.svg|right|400px|thumb|This plot shows a typical octahedral profile of several plasticity models: [[von Mises yield criterion|von Mises]], [[Drucker-Prager yield criterion|linear Drucker–Prager]], [[Mohr-Coulomb theory|Mohr–Coulomb]], [[Gurson yield criterion|Gurson]], and [[Yield surface#Bigoni.E2.80.93Piccolroaz yield surface|Bigoni–Piccolroaz]]. This plot has omitted Lode angle values in favor of loading descriptions because of the preponderance of definitions of the Lode angle. The radial coordinate is <math>r=\sqrt{2J_2}</math>.]]

The octahedral profile is a 2D plot of <math>(r,\theta)</math> holding <math>z</math> constant. Plotting the yield surface in the octahedral plane demonstrates the level of Lode angle dependence. The octahedral plane is sometimes referred to as the 'pi plane'<ref>Lubliner, Jacob; 1990, ''Plasticity Theory'', Pearson Education</ref> or 'deviatoric plane'.<ref>Chaboche, J.-L.; 2008, "A review of some plasticity and viscoplasticity theories", ''International Journal of Plasticity'', 24(10):1642-1693, DOI:10.1016/j.ijplas.2008.03.009</ref>

The octahedral profile is not necessarily constant for different values of pressure with the notable exceptions of the [[von Mises yield criterion]] and the [[Tresca yield criterion#Tresca yield surface|Tresca yield criterion]] which are constant for all values of pressure.

==A note on terminology==

The term ''Haigh-Westergaard space'' is ambiguously used in the literature to mean both the Cartesian principal stress space<ref>Mouazen, Abdul Mounem; Neményi, Miklós; 1998, "A review of the finite element modelling techniques of soil tillage", ''Mathematics and Computers in Simulation'', Volume 48, Issue 1, 1 November 1998, Pages 23-32, doi: 10.1016/S0378-4754(98)00152-9</ref><ref>Keryvin, Vincent; 2008, "Indentation as a probe for pressure sensitivity of metallic glasses", ''Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter'', Volume 20, Number 11, DOI: 10.1088/0953-8984/20/11/114119</ref> and the cylindrical Lode coordinate space<ref name="cervenka">Červenka, Jan; Papanikolaou, Vassilis K.; 2008, "Three dimensional combined fracture–plastic material model for concrete", ''International Journal of Plasticity'', Volume 24, Issue 12, December 2008, Pages 2192-2220, 
doi: 10.1016/j.ijplas.2008.01.004</ref><ref name="piccolroaz2009">Piccolroaz, Andrea; Bigoni, Davide; 2009, "Yield criteria for quasibrittle and frictional materials: A generalization to surfaces with corners", ''International Journal of Solids and Structures'', Volume 46, Issue 20, 1 October 2009, Pages 3587-3596, doi: 10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2009.06.006</ref>
